summary: Describes the frame format for IPv6 packets over IEEE 802.15.4 networks, how to form link-local and autoconfigured addresses, a simple header compression scheme, and mesh delivery. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Small sensors and other low-power devices use IEEE 802.15.4 radios, which send very small frames. IPv6 expects much larger packets. RFC 4944 explains how to send IPv6 over these radios anyway. It defines how to split large packets into pieces that fit, how to shrink headers so most messages fit in a single frame, and how devices form their IPv6 addresses from their radio addresses.

questions: how to send ipv6 over ieee 802.15.4
what is the ipv6 mtu on 802.15.4
subtitle: How to carry 1280-octet IPv6 packets over IEEE 802.15.4 radio frames that hold at most 102 octets at the MAC layer.

tldr.problem: IPv6 expects links that carry packets of at least 1280 octets, but an IEEE 802.15.4 physical packet is at most 127 octets, a MAC frame is at most 102 octets, and link-layer security leaves as few as 81.
tldr.mechanism: A thin adaptation layer called the LoWPAN encapsulation stacks mesh, broadcast and fragmentation headers before the payload, and a simple stateless header compression scheme shrinks the common IPv6 and UDP headers using what all devices on the link already share.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 can run on low-power radio networks; in the common case the 40-octet IPv6 header compresses to 2 octets. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6282, RFC 6775, RFC 8025, RFC 8066 and RFC 8931, and no RFC obsoletes it.

today: RFC 4944 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. It has been updated by RFC 6282, RFC 6775, RFC 8025, RFC 8066 and RFC 8931, and no RFC obsoletes it. Read those updates alongside this text when implementing.

sections.title: What This RFC Does
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.15.4 standard targets low-power personal area networks (PANs). RFC 4944 defines the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over such networks, and how to form IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on top of them. Because IPv6 expects far larger packets than an 802.15.4 frame can hold, the RFC defines an adaptation layer. It also defines a header compression scheme and the provisions needed to deliver packets across an 802.15.4 mesh; a full specification of mesh routing itself is explicitly out of scope.

IPv6 packets MUST be carried in 802.15.4 data frames, and the RFC recommends asking for link-layer acknowledgements to aid recovery. It does not require beacon-enabled mode: in nonbeacon-enabled networks, data frames are sent with unslotted CSMA/CA. Both the source and the destination addresses MUST be included in the 802.15.4 frame header. A personal area network (PAN) maps to one IPv6 link.
sections.plainLanguage: Battery-powered gadgets talk over tiny radio messages. This RFC explains how they can still use IPv6, the standard internet addressing scheme. It covers splitting messages, shrinking them and building addresses.

sections.title: Why the Frames Are Too Small
sections.content:
The IPv6 MTU defined here is 1280 octets. An 802.15.4 physical packet is at most 127 octets (aMaxPHYPacketSize), and with a maximum frame overhead of 25 octets (aMaxFrameOverhead) the largest MAC frame is 102 octets. Link-layer security takes more: 21 octets in the AES-CCM-128 case, versus 9 and 13 for AES-CCM-32 and AES-CCM-64, leaving only 81 octets available.

The 40-octet IPv6 header then leaves 41 octets for upper layers. UDP uses 8 of those, leaving 33 octets for application data, before any fragmentation overhead. The RFC draws two conclusions. First, an adaptation layer for fragmentation and reassembly is needed to meet IPv6's minimum MTU, though most applications are expected to use small payloads that fit in one frame once headers are compressed. Second, header compression is "compelling to the point of almost being unavoidable".
sections.plainLanguage: A letter will not fit through a mail slot made for postcards. You have to cut the letter into pieces, and it helps a lot to write in short-hand. This RFC does both.

sections.title: The LoWPAN Header Stack
sections.content:
Every LoWPAN datagram starts with a stack of encapsulation headers, each beginning with a type, and the LoWPAN payload (for example an IPv6 packet) follows. When more than one header is used they MUST appear in this order: Mesh Addressing Header, Broadcast Header, Fragmentation Header.

The first two bits of a header are its dispatch type. The dispatch value is an 8-bit selector: 00 marks a frame that is Not A LoWPAN frame (NALP), which any LoWPAN node discards; 01 000001 means an uncompressed IPv6 header follows; 01 000010 means a LOWPAN_HC1 compressed header; 01 010000 is the LOWPAN_BC0 broadcast header; 01 111111 (ESC) means an additional dispatch byte follows; 10 starts a mesh header; 11 000xxx is the first fragment header and 11 100xxx a subsequent one. Non-LoWPAN protocols that want to coexist should put a byte matching the NALP pattern right after the 802.15.4 header.

The mesh header begins with bits 1 0, then a V bit and an F bit saying whether the originator and final destination addresses are 64-bit EUI-64 (0) or 16-bit short (1) addresses, then a 4-bit Hops Left field. Each forwarder decrements Hops Left before sending, and the packet is not forwarded further when it reaches zero. The value 0xF is reserved and signals an 8-bit Deep Hops Left field immediately after, allowing a source to specify a hop limit greater than 14.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets labels stuck on the front in a fixed order, like a parcel with a route sticker, a pieces sticker, then the contents. The first bits of each label say what kind of label it is, so a node can tell at a glance what follows.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
If an entire payload datagram fits within a single 802.15.4 frame it is unfragmented and no fragmentation header is used. If it does not fit, it SHALL be broken into link fragments. Because the fragment offset can only express multiples of eight bytes, every fragment except the last one MUST be a multiple of eight bytes long, and the first fragment SHALL carry the first fragment header.

The first fragment header holds an 11-bit datagram_size and a 16-bit datagram_tag; subsequent fragments add an 8-bit datagram_offset. The size is that of the whole IP packet before link fragmentation, which for IPv6 is 40 octets more than the Payload Length, up to the 1280-octet link MTU. The tag is the same for all fragments of one datagram, is incremented for each successive fragmented datagram and wraps from 65535 back to zero. Carrying the size in every fragment eases reassembly when a later fragment arrives before the first one.

A recipient identifies fragments of one datagram by the sender's 802.15.4 source address (or the mesh Originator Address), the destination address (or the Final Destination address), datagram_size and datagram_tag, and reassembles into a buffer sized from datagram_size. If an overlapping fragment differs in size or offset, the accumulated fragments SHALL be discarded. On an 802.15.4 Disassociation event, partial reassemblies MUST be discarded on both sides. The reassembly timer MUST be set to a maximum of 60 seconds, the same timeout as IPv6 reassembly.
sections.plainLanguage: A big message is cut into puzzle pieces. Each piece says which message it belongs to and where it fits. If the missing pieces do not arrive within 60 seconds, the receiver throws the half-built message away.

sections.title: Addresses, Link-Local and Multicast
sections.content:
IEEE 802.15.4 defines two addressing modes: 64-bit extended addresses (EUI-64) and, after an association event, 16-bit short addresses unique within the PAN. The RFC supports both, and warns that short addresses are transient: their validity lasts only as long as the association, and the PAN coordinator that hands them out is a scalability limit and a single point of failure. Within 6LoWPANs, 16-bit short addresses MUST follow a defined format: a leading 0 bit for unicast, the pattern 100 for multicast, and the rest reserved for future assignment.

The interface identifier may be based on the EUI-64, formed as in "IPv6 over Ethernet" (RFC 2464). When a short address is used instead, a pseudo 48-bit address is built from 16 zero bits, the 16-bit PAN ID (or 16 zero bits if none is known) and the 16-bit short address; the resulting interface identifier has its U/L bit set to zero, because the value is not globally unique. All-zero addresses MUST NOT be used. A prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration MUST be 64 bits long, and the link-local address is the interface identifier appended to the FE80::/64 prefix.

802.15.4 has no native multicast, so IPv6 multicast MUST be carried as link-layer broadcast: the frame's destination PAN ID must match the link's, and the short destination address must be 0xffff. Inside a mesh-enabled LoWPAN, an IPv6 multicast destination maps to a 16-bit address of the form 100 followed by the last 5 bits of DST[15] and all of DST[16].
sections.plainLanguage: Every gadget has a long serial number and may also get a short nickname from the network's coordinator. The IPv6 name is built from one of them. To reach everyone at once, the gadget broadcasts to the whole radio group.

sections.title: Header Compression (HC1 and HC_UDP)
sections.content:
Compression here is deliberately simple. Devices on the same 6LoWPAN network share state simply by having joined, so the scheme keeps no per-flow context and relies on information about the whole link. The LOWPAN_HC1 encoding assumes the common case: the version is IPv6, both addresses are link local, the interface identifiers can be inferred from the layer two addresses, the packet length can be inferred from the frame or the datagram_size field, Traffic Class and Flow Label are zero, and the Next Header is UDP, ICMP or TCP. Only the 8-bit Hop Limit always needs to be carried in full, so this common header compresses to 2 octets (one for the HC1 encoding, one for the Hop Limit) instead of 40.

The 8-bit HC1 encoding field uses two bits each for the source and destination address (prefix carried in-line or compressed to the link-local prefix; interface identifier carried in-line or elided as derivable from the link-layer address), one bit for Traffic Class and Flow Label, two bits for Next Header (not compressed, UDP, ICMP, TCP) and one bit saying an HC2 encoding immediately follows.

For UDP, the HC_UDP encoding can compress each 16-bit port to 4 bits by adding a short value to the base 61616 (0xF0B0), and can drop the length, which is derived from the IPv6 Payload Length minus any extension headers. The checksum is never compressed and is always carried in full, so the UDP header shrinks to 4 octets from 8. When compression leaves fields misaligned, zero bits are added so that subsequent fields start on an octet boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone on the network already knows the usual address, you do not need to write it on every note. You tick a box that means "same as usual" and only write what is different. A tick and one number can replace a 40-octet header.

sections.title: Delivery Across a Mesh
sections.content:
IEEE 802.15.4 does not itself define mesh routing, so the RFC adds a way to carry end-to-end link-layer addresses. A node that cannot reach the destination directly MUST include a Mesh Addressing header with the Originator Address set to its own link-layer address and the Final Destination Address set to the packet's ultimate target, then send the frame to a default forwarder: the 802.15.4 source is its own address and the 802.15.4 destination is the forwarder's.

A receiving node reads the Final Destination field. If it is itself the final destination it consumes the packet as usual. Otherwise it decrements Hops Left, discards the packet if the result is zero, consults its link-layer routing table for the next hop towards the final destination, puts that address in the 802.15.4 destination field, sets the source to its own address, and transmits. Only Full Function Devices (FFDs) are expected to participate as mesh routers. Reduced Function Devices (RFDs) limit themselves to discovering FFDs and using them as forwarders, in the way IP hosts use default routers.

A broadcast header (dispatch LOWPAN_BC0) adds an 8-bit sequence number that the originator increments whenever it sends a new mesh broadcast or multicast packet, so duplicates can be detected. Detailed broadcast handling and mesh routing protocols are out of scope. Appendix A explains why mesh delivery uses link-layer rather than IP addresses: with IP-based delivery, fragments arriving out of order would force intermediate nodes to buffer until the first fragment arrives, and the approach would only work for IPv6 payloads.
sections.plainLanguage: Pass the parcel: each node knows the final recipient, hands the message to a neighbour that is closer, and drops it if it has been passed too many times. Full-function devices do the passing; simple devices just hand their messages to one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Interface identifiers derived from EUI-64 addresses are intended to preserve global uniqueness when possible, but there is no protection from duplication through accident or forgery. Neighbor Discovery on IEEE 802.15.4 links may face the threats described in RFC 3756, and mesh routing is expected to be common, which adds further threats from ad hoc routing.

IEEE 802.15.4 provides link-layer security using AES modes for authentication or encryption of frames, but does not specify key management. The RFC urges users to make use of link-layer security where possible and practical. A sizeable portion of 802.15.4 devices will communicate only within their PAN and implement the minimum feature set, so their security may rely strongly on the link layer. Full Function Devices that also talk to off-link IPv6 peers are expected to secure those end-to-end communications with the usual mechanisms such as IPsec or TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The radio can lock its messages, but the RFC does not say who hands out the keys. People who build a network must plan that part themselves, and gadgets that talk to the wider internet should lock those conversations too.

items.title: IPv6 MTU
items.text: 1280 octets is the minimum packet size IPv6 links must carry.

items.title: MAC frame
items.text: 102 octets after the 25-octet maximum frame overhead.

items.title: With AES-CCM-128
items.text: 21 octets of security overhead leave only 81 octets.

items.title: IPv6 header
items.text: 40 octets, leaving 41 for upper layers before fragmentation.

items.title: UDP payload
items.text: UDP uses 8 octets, leaving 33 octets for application data.

fields.name: Pattern 11000
fields.desc: Dispatch bits that identify the first fragment header.

fields.name: datagram_size
fields.desc: Size of the whole IP packet before link-layer fragmentation; same for all fragments.

fields.name: datagram_tag
fields.desc: Same for all fragments of one datagram; incremented per successive fragmented datagram, wraps at 65535.

items.label: Source address
items.desc: 00 PI,II; 01 PI,IC; 10 PC,II; 11 PC,IC (prefix carried or compressed to link-local; interface identifier carried or elided).

items.label: Destination address
items.desc: The same four combinations as the source address.

items.label: Traffic Class and Flow Label
items.desc: 1 means both are zero; 0 means the full 8 bits and 20 bits are sent.

items.label: Next Header
items.desc: 00 sent in full; 01 UDP; 10 ICMP; 11 TCP.

items.label: HC2 encoding
items.desc: 1 means more compression bits (such as HC_UDP) immediately follow.
